cards.q: Define the amplitude of a wave.
cards.a: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its equilibrium (undisturbed) position.
cards.why: It is measured from the centre line to a peak, not from trough to peak.

cards.q: Define the frequency and the period of a wave, and state how they are related.
cards.a: Frequency: the number of complete oscillations per unit time. Period: the time for one complete oscillation. f=1T\displaystyle f = \frac{1}{T}f=T1​.

cards.q: Define the wavelength of a wave.
cards.a: The shortest distance between two points that are in phase, for example from one peak to the next.

cards.q: What does a progressive wave transfer, and what does it not transfer?
cards.a: It transfers energy. It does not transfer matter: the particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions.

cards.q: Sound travels at 340 m s−1\displaystyle 340\ \text{m s}^{-1}340 m s−1 in air. Calculate the wavelength of a 500 Hz note.
cards.a: 0.68 m
steps: Rearrange the wave equation: λ=vf\displaystyle \lambda = \frac{v}{f}λ=fv​.
λ=340500\displaystyle \lambda = \frac{340}{500}λ=500340​
λ=0.68 m\displaystyle \lambda = 0.68\ \text{m}λ=0.68 m

cards.q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate its period.
cards.a: 0.020 s
steps: T=1f=150\displaystyle T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{50}T=f1​=501​
T=0.020 s\displaystyle T = 0.020\ \text{s}T=0.020 s

cards.q: What is meant by the phase difference between two points on a wave?
cards.a: The fraction of a cycle by which one point's oscillation leads or lags the other's. It is given as a fraction of a cycle or as an angle, in degrees or radians.
cards.why: One full cycle is 360°, or 2π\displaystyle 2\pi2π radians.

cards.q: What phase difference do two points have when they are in phase, and when they are in antiphase?
cards.a: In phase: 0, or a whole number of cycles (360°, 2π\displaystyle 2\pi2π rad). In antiphase: half a cycle (180°, π\displaystyle \piπ rad).

cards.q: Two points on a wave are a distance x\displaystyle xx apart along the direction of travel. Write their phase difference in radians.
cards.a: phase difference=2πxλ\displaystyle \text{phase difference} = \frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}phase difference=λ2πx​
cards.why: A distance of one wavelength is one whole cycle, 2π\displaystyle 2\pi2π radians.

cards.q: Two points on a wave of wavelength 0.80 m are 0.20 m apart. Calculate their phase difference in degrees.
cards.a: 90°
steps: Fraction of a wavelength: 0.200.80=0.25\displaystyle \frac{0.20}{0.80} = 0.250.800.20​=0.25.
A quarter of a cycle: 0.25×360∘\displaystyle 0.25 \times 360^\circ0.25×360∘
=90∘\displaystyle = 90^\circ=90∘ (π2\displaystyle \frac{\pi}{2}2π​ rad)

cards.q: A wave is shown on a displacement–distance graph and on a displacement–time graph. Which quantity can be read from the repeat length of each?
cards.a: Displacement–distance: the wavelength. Displacement–time: the period.
cards.why: Check the horizontal axis before reading anything off a wave graph.

cards.q: What is a transverse wave? Give two examples.
cards.a: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. Examples: electromagnetic waves, waves on a string.

cards.q: What is a longitudinal wave? Give an example.
cards.a: A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, producing compressions and rarefactions. Example: sound.

cards.q: In a sound wave, where is the pressure greatest, and what is the displacement of the molecules at that point?
cards.a: The pressure is greatest at the centre of a compression. There the displacement of the molecules is zero: molecules on either side have moved towards it.
cards.why: Pressure and displacement are a quarter of a cycle out of step.

cards.q: What do all electromagnetic waves have in common when they travel through a vacuum?
cards.a: They all travel at the same speed, 3.00×108 m s−1\displaystyle 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}3.00×108 m s−1, and they are all transverse.

cards.q: What is a plane-polarised wave?
cards.a: A transverse wave whose oscillations are confined to a single plane, the plane containing the direction of travel.

cards.q: Why is polarisation evidence that light is a transverse wave?
cards.a: Only transverse waves can be polarised. In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are along the direction of travel, so there is no plane to restrict them to.

cards.q: Unpolarised light passes through two polarising filters. Describe what is seen as the second filter is rotated through 360°.
cards.a: The transmitted intensity varies from a maximum when the filters are aligned to zero when they are at 90° (crossed), twice in each full turn.

cards.q: Give two applications of polarisation.
cards.a: Polaroid sunglasses reduce glare, because light reflected from surfaces such as water is partly polarised. Aerials for radio and television are aligned with the plane of polarisation of the transmitted signal.

cards.q: State the principle of superposition.
cards.a: When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements of the individual waves.

cards.q: Explain how a stationary wave is formed on a stretched string.
cards.a: Two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions superpose.
marks: A wave travels along the string and is reflected at the fixed end.
The reflected wave and the incoming wave have the same frequency (and wavelength) and travel in opposite directions.
The two waves superpose.
Where they always cancel there are nodes; where they always reinforce there are antinodes.

cards.q: What are a node and an antinode on a stationary wave?
cards.a: A node is a point of zero amplitude. An antinode is a point of maximum amplitude.

cards.q: On a stationary wave, what is the distance between two adjacent nodes?
cards.a: Half a wavelength, λ2\displaystyle \frac{\lambda}{2}2λ​.
cards.why: A node to the next antinode is a quarter of a wavelength.

cards.q: Give three differences between a stationary wave and a progressive wave.
cards.a: They differ in energy transfer, amplitude and phase.
marks: Energy: a progressive wave transfers energy; a stationary wave does not transfer energy along its length.
Amplitude: in a progressive wave every point has the same amplitude; in a stationary wave it varies from zero at nodes to a maximum at antinodes.
Phase: in a progressive wave phase changes steadily along the wave; in a stationary wave all points between two adjacent nodes are in phase.

cards.q: On a stationary wave, what is the phase difference between two points on opposite sides of a node, in adjacent loops?
cards.a: 180° (π\displaystyle \piπ rad): they are in antiphase. Points within the same loop are in phase.

cards.q: A string of length l\displaystyle ll fixed at both ends vibrates in its first harmonic. What is the wavelength of the stationary wave?
cards.a: λ=2l\displaystyle \lambda = 2lλ=2l: the string holds half a wavelength, with a node at each end and one antinode in the middle.

cards.q: Write the equation for the frequency of the first harmonic of a stretched string, and say what each symbol means.
cards.a: f=12lTμ\displaystyle f = \frac{1}{2l}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}f=2l1​μT​​, where l\displaystyle ll is the length of the string, T\displaystyle TT the tension and μ\displaystyle \muμ the mass per unit length.
cards.why: It combines λ=2l\displaystyle \lambda = 2lλ=2l with the wave speed on the string, Tμ\displaystyle \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}μT​​.

cards.q: Write the equation for the speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string.
cards.a: v=Tμ\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}v=μT​​, where T\displaystyle TT is the tension and μ\displaystyle \muμ is the mass per unit length of the string.

cards.q: A string has a mass per unit length of 4.0×10−3 kg m−1\displaystyle 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^{-1}4.0×10−3 kg m−1 and is under a tension of 40 N. Calculate the speed of transverse waves along it.
cards.a: 100 m s−1\displaystyle 100\ \text{m s}^{-1}100 m s−1
steps: v=Tμ=404.0×10−3\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\frac{40}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}}v=μT​​=4.0×10−340​​
v=1.0×104=100 m s−1\displaystyle v = \sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{4}} = 100\ \text{m s}^{-1}v=1.0×104​=100 m s−1

cards.q: A string 0.60 m long has a mass per unit length of 2.0×10−3 kg m−1\displaystyle 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^{-1}2.0×10−3 kg m−1 and a tension of 50 N. Calculate the frequency of its first harmonic.
cards.a: 130 Hz
steps: Wave speed: v=Tμ=502.0×10−3=158 m s−1\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\frac{50}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}} = 158\ \text{m s}^{-1}v=μT​​=2.0×10−350​​=158 m s−1.
First harmonic: λ=2l=1.2 m\displaystyle \lambda = 2l = 1.2\ \text{m}λ=2l=1.2 m.
f=vλ=1581.2=130 Hz\displaystyle f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{158}{1.2} = 130\ \text{Hz}f=λv​=1.2158​=130 Hz

cards.q: A string vibrates in its first harmonic at frequency f\displaystyle ff. What are the frequencies of its second and third harmonics, and how many antinodes does each have?
cards.a: Second harmonic: 2f\displaystyle 2f2f, with two antinodes. Third harmonic: 3f\displaystyle 3f3f, with three antinodes.
cards.why: The n\displaystyle nnth harmonic fits n\displaystyle nn half-wavelengths on the string.

cards.q: The tension in a string is made four times larger, with its length unchanged. How does the frequency of its first harmonic change?
cards.a: It doubles.
cards.why: f∝T\displaystyle f \propto \sqrt{T}f∝T​, and 4=2\displaystyle \sqrt{4} = 24​=2.

cards.q: Outline how to investigate how the frequency of the first harmonic of a stretched string depends on its length.
cards.a: Set up a stationary wave with a vibration generator and find the first-harmonic frequency for each length.
marks: Attach a string to a vibration generator driven by a signal generator, and pass it over a pulley to a hanging mass that sets the tension.
Adjust the frequency until the string vibrates in one loop (the first harmonic), and record the frequency.
Measure the vibrating length l\displaystyle ll with a metre rule.
Repeat for a range of lengths, keeping the tension and the string (mass per unit length) the same.
Plot f\displaystyle ff against 1l\displaystyle \frac{1}{l}l1​: a straight line through the origin.

cards.q: In the vibrating string experiment, the tension T\displaystyle TT is varied at constant length. What graph gives a straight line through the origin?
cards.a: f\displaystyle ff against T\displaystyle \sqrt{T}T​ (or f2\displaystyle f^{2}f2 against T\displaystyle TT).
cards.afig: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 250" role="img" aria-label="Frequency against the square root of tension for a stretched string: a straight line through the origin." class="pg-svg"><rect x="0" y="0" width="360" height="250" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#d8d8d8"/><path d="M52 204 L346 204 M52 204 L52 12" fill="none" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M351 204 l-7 -4 v8 Z M52 7 l-4 7 h8 Z" fill="#1a1a1a"/><text x="195" y="240" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a">√T  (T is the tension)</text><text x="14" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a" transform="rotate(-90 14 112)">frequency</text><text x="44" y="219" text-anchor="end" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a">0</text><path d="M52 204 L312 53.5" fill="none" stroke="#0b4fa8" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/></svg>
cards.why: f=12lTμ\displaystyle f = \frac{1}{2l}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}f=2l1​μT​​, so f∝T\displaystyle f \propto \sqrt{T}f∝T​.

cards.q: Describe how a stationary wave can be set up and investigated using microwaves.
cards.a: Reflect the microwaves back along their own path and move a detector between the transmitter and the reflector.
marks: Point a microwave transmitter at a metal plate, which reflects the waves back.
The outgoing and reflected waves superpose to form a stationary wave.
Move a probe detector along the line between them: the signal falls to a minimum at each node and rises to a maximum at each antinode.
The distance between adjacent nodes is half a wavelength.

cards.q: Outline how to determine the speed of sound in air using a two-beam oscilloscope, a signal generator, a loudspeaker and a microphone.
cards.a: Find the wavelength by moving the microphone until its trace is back in phase with the signal, then use v=fλ\displaystyle v = f\lambdav=fλ.
marks: Connect the signal generator to the loudspeaker and to one input of the oscilloscope; connect the microphone to the other input.
Place the microphone so the two traces are in phase.
Move the microphone away until the traces are next in phase: the distance moved is one wavelength.
Move through several wavelengths and divide, to reduce the uncertainty.
Read the frequency from the signal generator (or from the oscilloscope) and calculate v=fλ\displaystyle v = f\lambdav=fλ.

cards.q: What does it mean to say that two wave sources are coherent?
cards.a: They have a constant phase difference, which requires the same frequency.

cards.q: What is meant by path difference?
cards.a: The difference in the distances travelled by two waves from their sources to the point where they meet.

cards.q: Waves from two coherent sources that are in phase meet at a point. State the path difference needed for constructive interference, and for destructive interference.
cards.a: Constructive: a whole number of wavelengths, nλ\displaystyle n\lambdanλ. Destructive: an odd number of half-wavelengths, (n+12)λ\displaystyle (n + \frac{1}{2})\lambda(n+21​)λ.

cards.q: What is monochromatic light?
cards.a: Light of a single wavelength (a single frequency).

cards.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, why is light from a single source passed through two slits?
cards.a: The two slits then act as coherent sources: light from them comes from the same wave, so they have a constant phase difference and a steady interference pattern forms.
cards.why: Two separate lamps are not coherent, so their pattern would shift too quickly to be seen.

cards.q: In the double-slit equation w=λDs\displaystyle w = \frac{\lambda D}{s}w=sλD​, what does each symbol stand for?
cards.a: w\displaystyle ww: fringe spacing. λ\displaystyle \lambdaλ: wavelength of the light. D\displaystyle DD: distance from the slits to the screen. s\displaystyle ss: separation of the two slits.

cards.q: Light of wavelength 650 nm passes through two slits 0.50 mm apart and falls on a screen 2.0 m away. Calculate the fringe spacing.
cards.a: 2.6×10−3 m\displaystyle 2.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}2.6×10−3 m (2.6 mm)
steps: Convert: λ=650×10−9 m\displaystyle \lambda = 650 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{m}λ=650×10−9 m, s=0.50×10−3 m\displaystyle s = 0.50 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}s=0.50×10−3 m.
w=λDs=650×10−9×2.00.50×10−3\displaystyle w = \frac{\lambda D}{s} = \frac{650 \times 10^{-9} \times 2.0}{0.50 \times 10^{-3}}w=sλD​=0.50×10−3650×10−9×2.0​
w=2.6×10−3 m\displaystyle w = 2.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}w=2.6×10−3 m

cards.q: In a double-slit experiment, what happens to the fringe spacing if the slits are moved closer together?
cards.a: The fringes become further apart.
cards.why: w=λDs\displaystyle w = \frac{\lambda D}{s}w=sλD​: a smaller slit separation s\displaystyle ss gives a larger spacing w\displaystyle ww.

cards.q: Describe the double-slit interference pattern produced with white light.
cards.a: A white central fringe, with coloured fringes either side: each is blue on the side nearer the centre and red on the outside. Further out the colours overlap and the pattern fades.
cards.why: Fringe spacing depends on wavelength, so each colour makes its own pattern. Only at the centre do they all coincide.

cards.q: State two safety precautions when using a laser in the laboratory.
cards.a: Never look directly into the beam, and avoid reflections of it: keep shiny surfaces out of its path. Also, a warning sign and a laser pointed away from where people sit or enter.

cards.q: Why is a laser a suitable light source for interference experiments?
cards.a: Its light is monochromatic and coherent, so it gives clear, sharp fringes.

cards.q: Two loudspeakers are connected to the same signal generator. A student walking along a line in front of them hears the sound rise and fall. Explain why.
cards.a: The sound waves from the two speakers interfere.
marks: The two speakers are coherent sources, because they are driven by the same signal.
At each point the waves have travelled different distances: there is a path difference.
Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths the waves arrive in phase and reinforce: the sound is loud.
Where it is an odd number of half-wavelengths they arrive in antiphase and cancel: the sound is quiet.

cards.q: In a double-slit experiment, how should the fringe spacing be measured to keep its uncertainty small?
cards.a: Measure the distance across several fringes (for example ten) and divide by the number of spacings.
cards.why: The same absolute uncertainty is spread over many fringes, so the percentage uncertainty is smaller.

cards.q: What is diffraction?
cards.a: The spreading out of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle.

cards.q: For which size of gap does a wave diffract the most?
cards.a: When the width of the gap is about the same as the wavelength.
cards.why: A gap much wider than the wavelength gives very little spreading.

cards.q: State Huygens' construction.
cards.a: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. The new wavefront is the surface that touches all these wavelets.
cards.why: At a slit only part of the wavefront gets through, so its wavelets spread into the region beyond: this is diffraction.

cards.q: Describe the diffraction pattern produced when monochromatic light passes through a single narrow slit.
cards.a: A bright central maximum, twice as wide as the others, with fainter, narrower fringes on either side, separated by dark fringes.

cards.q: How does the width of the central maximum of a single-slit pattern change if the slit is made narrower, or the wavelength longer?
cards.a: In both cases the central maximum becomes wider.
cards.why: A narrower slit, or a longer wavelength, means more diffraction.

cards.q: Describe the single-slit diffraction pattern produced with white light.
cards.a: A white central maximum with coloured fringes on either side. In each side fringe, blue is nearer the centre and red is further out.

cards.q: In the diffraction grating equation dsin⁡θ=nλ\displaystyle d\sin\theta = n\lambdadsinθ=nλ, what does each symbol stand for?
cards.a: d\displaystyle dd: spacing between adjacent slits. θ\displaystyle \thetaθ: angle between the beam and the straight-through direction. n\displaystyle nn: order of the maximum. λ\displaystyle \lambdaλ: wavelength.

cards.q: Derive the diffraction grating equation dsin⁡θ=nλ\displaystyle d\sin\theta = n\lambdadsinθ=nλ.
cards.a: dsin⁡θ=nλ\displaystyle d\sin\theta = n\lambdadsinθ=nλ
steps: Consider light leaving two adjacent slits, a distance d\displaystyle dd apart, at an angle θ\displaystyle \thetaθ to the straight-through direction.
The path difference between the two rays is dsin⁡θ\displaystyle d\sin\thetadsinθ.
A maximum forms where rays from all the slits arrive in phase.
That needs the path difference to be a whole number of wavelengths: dsin⁡θ=nλ\displaystyle d\sin\theta = n\lambdadsinθ=nλ.

cards.q: A grating is labelled 300 lines per millimetre. A student uses d=300\displaystyle d = 300d=300. What should d\displaystyle dd be?
cards.a: d\displaystyle dd is the slit spacing, the reciprocal of the number of lines per metre: d=1300×103=3.3×10−6 m\displaystyle d = \frac{1}{300 \times 10^{3}} = 3.3 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}d=300×1031​=3.3×10−6 m.
cards.why: Convert lines per millimetre to lines per metre first, then take the reciprocal.

cards.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a grating with 300 lines per millimetre. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum.
cards.a: 10°
steps: Slit spacing: d=1300×103=3.33×10−6 m\displaystyle d = \frac{1}{300 \times 10^{3}} = 3.33 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}d=300×1031​=3.33×10−6 m.
sin⁡θ=nλd=1×600×10−93.33×10−6=0.180\displaystyle \sin\theta = \frac{n\lambda}{d} = \frac{1 \times 600 \times 10^{-9}}{3.33 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.180sinθ=dnλ​=3.33×10−61×600×10−9​=0.180
θ=10∘\displaystyle \theta = 10^\circθ=10∘

cards.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a grating of slit spacing 3.33×10−6 m\displaystyle 3.33 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}3.33×10−6 m. What is the highest order that can be seen?
cards.a: The 5th order
cards.why: Always round down: the sixth order would need sin⁡θ>1\displaystyle \sin\theta > 1sinθ>1.
steps: sin⁡θ\displaystyle \sin\thetasinθ cannot be greater than 1, so n≤dλ\displaystyle n \le \frac{d}{\lambda}n≤λd​.
dλ=3.33×10−6600×10−9=5.6\displaystyle \frac{d}{\lambda} = \frac{3.33 \times 10^{-6}}{600 \times 10^{-9}} = 5.6λd​=600×10−93.33×10−6​=5.6
n\displaystyle nn must be a whole number, so round down: n=5\displaystyle n = 5n=5.

cards.q: Outline how to determine the wavelength of laser light using a diffraction grating.
cards.a: Measure the angle of one of the orders and use the grating equation.
marks: Shine the laser at normal incidence through the grating onto a screen a measured distance D\displaystyle DD away.
Measure the distance x\displaystyle xx from the central maximum to the n\displaystyle nnth-order maximum.
Find the angle from tan⁡θ=xD\displaystyle \tan\theta = \frac{x}{D}tanθ=Dx​.
Find the slit spacing d\displaystyle dd from the number of lines per metre.
Calculate λ=dsin⁡θn\displaystyle \lambda = \frac{d\sin\theta}{n}λ=ndsinθ​, and repeat for other orders.

cards.q: Give an application of diffraction gratings.
cards.a: Analysing spectra: a grating separates light into its wavelengths, so the elements in a source such as a star can be identified from its spectral lines.

cards.q: Why does a diffraction grating give a more accurate value for wavelength than a double slit?
cards.a: Its maxima are much sharper and brighter, and further apart, so their positions can be measured with a smaller percentage uncertainty.

cards.q: Define the refractive index of a substance.
cards.a: The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the substance: n=ccs\displaystyle n = \frac{c}{c_{s}}n=cs​c​.
cards.why: It is never less than 1, and has no unit. For air it is approximately 1.

cards.q: State Snell's law for light crossing a boundary between two media.
cards.a: n1sin⁡θ1=n2sin⁡θ2\displaystyle n_{1}\sin\theta_{1} = n_{2}\sin\theta_{2}n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​, where the angles are measured from the normal.

cards.q: Light travelling in air meets a glass block of refractive index 1.50 at an angle of incidence of 40°. Calculate the angle of refraction.
cards.a: 25°
cards.why: Entering a more optically dense medium, the ray bends towards the normal, so the angle must come out smaller.
steps: n1sin⁡θ1=n2sin⁡θ2\displaystyle n_{1}\sin\theta_{1} = n_{2}\sin\theta_{2}n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​, with n1=1.00\displaystyle n_{1} = 1.00n1​=1.00 for air.
sin⁡θ2=1.00×sin⁡40∘1.50=0.429\displaystyle \sin\theta_{2} = \frac{1.00 \times \sin 40^\circ}{1.50} = 0.429sinθ2​=1.501.00×sin40∘​=0.429
θ2=25∘\displaystyle \theta_{2} = 25^\circθ2​=25∘

cards.q: Light passes from air into glass. What happens to its speed, its frequency and its wavelength?
cards.a: Its speed decreases, its frequency stays the same, and so its wavelength decreases.
cards.why: The frequency is set by the source. With v=fλ\displaystyle v = f\lambdav=fλ, a lower speed at the same frequency means a shorter wavelength.

cards.q: State the two conditions needed for total internal reflection.
cards.a: The light must be travelling from a medium of higher refractive index towards one of lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle.

cards.q: What is the critical angle?
cards.a: The angle of incidence, in the more optically dense medium, for which the angle of refraction is 90°.

cards.q: Write the equation for the critical angle at a boundary between a medium of refractive index n1\displaystyle n_{1}n1​ and a less dense medium of refractive index n2\displaystyle n_{2}n2​.
cards.a: sin⁡θc=n2n1\displaystyle \sin\theta_{c} = \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}}sinθc​=n1​n2​​. For a boundary with air this becomes sin⁡θc=1n\displaystyle \sin\theta_{c} = \frac{1}{n}sinθc​=n1​.

cards.q: Calculate the critical angle for a boundary between glass of refractive index 1.50 and air.
cards.a: 42°
steps: sin⁡θc=1n=11.50=0.667\displaystyle \sin\theta_{c} = \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{1.50} = 0.667sinθc​=n1​=1.501​=0.667
θc=42∘\displaystyle \theta_{c} = 42^\circθc​=42∘

cards.q: An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.50 and cladding of refractive index 1.45. Calculate the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary.
cards.a: 75°
cards.why: The smaller number goes on top: the sine cannot be greater than 1.

cards.q: Give two functions of the cladding in a step-index optical fibre.
cards.a: It has a lower refractive index than the core, so light is totally internally reflected at the boundary. It also protects the core from scratches and stops light crossing between fibres that touch.

cards.q: What is modal dispersion in an optical fibre, and how is it reduced?
cards.a: Light rays enter at different angles and so travel different path lengths along the fibre, arriving at different times. It is reduced by using a very narrow core.

cards.q: What is material dispersion in an optical fibre, and how is it reduced?
cards.a: Different wavelengths travel at different speeds in the glass, so they arrive at different times. It is reduced by using monochromatic light.

cards.q: What is pulse broadening in an optical fibre, and why does it matter?
cards.a: A pulse spreads out in time as it travels, because of dispersion. If pulses spread enough to overlap, the information they carry is lost, which limits how quickly pulses can be sent and how long the fibre can be.

cards.q: What is absorption in an optical fibre, and what is its effect on the signal?
cards.a: Some of the signal's energy is absorbed by the glass, so the amplitude of the pulses decreases along the fibre.

cards.q: Outline how to measure the refractive index of a rectangular glass block.
cards.a: Trace rays through the block for several angles of incidence and plot the sines of the angles.
marks: Place the block on paper, draw round it, and shine a narrow ray from a ray box into one side.
Mark the incident ray and the emergent ray, remove the block and join the points to show the path inside.
Draw the normal and measure the angle of incidence i\displaystyle ii and the angle of refraction r\displaystyle rr with a protractor.
Repeat for a range of angles of incidence.
Plot sin⁡i\displaystyle \sin isini against sin⁡r\displaystyle \sin rsinr: the gradient is the refractive index.

cards.q: What happens to a wave when it meets an interface between two media?
cards.a: Part of it is transmitted into the second medium and part is reflected.

cards.q: Define the focal length of a converging lens.
cards.a: The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus: the point where rays parallel to the principal axis converge after passing through the lens.

cards.q: What is the principal focus of a diverging lens?
cards.a: The point from which rays parallel to the principal axis appear to diverge after passing through the lens. It is on the same side as the incoming light, so the focal length is taken as negative.

cards.q: Define the power of a lens, and state its unit.
cards.a: P=1f\displaystyle P = \frac{1}{f}P=f1​, with the focal length f\displaystyle ff in metres. Unit: the dioptre, D.

cards.q: A converging lens has a focal length of 25 cm. Calculate its power.
cards.a: 4.0 D
cards.why: Leaving the focal length in centimetres is the usual slip.
steps: Convert the focal length to metres: f=0.25 m\displaystyle f = 0.25\ \text{m}f=0.25 m.
P=1f=10.25\displaystyle P = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{0.25}P=f1​=0.251​
P=4.0 D\displaystyle P = 4.0\ \text{D}P=4.0 D

cards.q: Two thin lenses of powers P1\displaystyle P_{1}P1​ and P2\displaystyle P_{2}P2​ are placed in contact. What is the power of the combination?
cards.a: P=P1+P2\displaystyle P = P_{1} + P_{2}P=P1​+P2​
cards.why: A diverging lens has a negative power, so it reduces the total.

cards.q: What is the difference between a real image and a virtual image?
cards.a: A real image is formed where rays of light actually meet, so it can be shown on a screen. A virtual image is where rays only appear to come from: it cannot be shown on a screen.

cards.q: Write the thin lens equation, and state the sign convention used with it.
cards.a: 1u+1v=1f\displaystyle \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f}u1​+v1​=f1​, where u\displaystyle uu is the object distance and v\displaystyle vv the image distance. Real is positive: distances to real objects and images are positive, and to virtual images negative.

cards.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Calculate the image distance.
cards.a: 15 cm, a real image.
cards.why: All three distances may stay in centimetres, as long as they are all in the same unit.

1v=330−130=230\displaystyle \frac{1}{v} = \frac{3}{30} - \frac{1}{30} = \frac{2}{30}v1​=303​−301​=302​
v=15 cm\displaystyle v = 15\ \text{cm}v=15 cm. It is positive, so the image is real.

cards.q: An object is placed 5.0 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Calculate the image distance and say what kind of image it is.
cards.a: v=−10 cm\displaystyle v = -10\ \text{cm}v=−10 cm: a virtual image, on the same side as the object.
cards.why: An object closer than the focal length gives a magnified virtual image: this is a magnifying glass.

v=−10 cm\displaystyle v = -10\ \text{cm}v=−10 cm. The negative sign means the image is virtual.

cards.q: Write two expressions for the magnification produced by a lens.
cards.a: m=image heightobject height\displaystyle m = \frac{\text{image height}}{\text{object height}}m=object heightimage height​ and m=vu\displaystyle m = \frac{v}{u}m=uv​.

cards.q: State the paths of the two rays normally drawn from the top of an object to locate its image in a converging lens.
cards.a: A ray parallel to the principal axis is refracted through the principal focus. A ray through the centre of the lens continues undeviated. The image is where they cross.

cards.q: Define the intensity of radiation, and state its unit.
cards.a: The power per unit area, where the area is perpendicular to the direction of travel: I=PA\displaystyle I = \frac{P}{A}I=AP​. Unit: W m−2\displaystyle \text{W m}^{-2}W m−2.

cards.q: A lamp radiates 60 W of light uniformly in all directions. Calculate the intensity 2.0 m from the lamp.
cards.a: 1.2 W m−2\displaystyle 1.2\ \text{W m}^{-2}1.2 W m−2
cards.why: The surface area of a sphere, 4πr2\displaystyle 4\pi r^{2}4πr2, is not on the formulae sheet.
steps: The power spreads over a sphere of area 4πr2=4π×2.02=50.3 m2\displaystyle 4\pi r^{2} = 4\pi \times 2.0^{2} = 50.3\ \text{m}^{2}4πr2=4π×2.02=50.3 m2.
I=PA=6050.3\displaystyle I = \frac{P}{A} = \frac{60}{50.3}I=AP​=50.360​
I=1.2 W m−2\displaystyle I = 1.2\ \text{W m}^{-2}I=1.2 W m−2

cards.q: An ultrasound pulse travels at 1500 m s−1\displaystyle 1500\ \text{m s}^{-1}1500 m s−1 in tissue. Its echo from a boundary returns 4.0×10−5 s\displaystyle 4.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{s}4.0×10−5 s after it was sent. Calculate the depth of the boundary.
cards.a: 0.030 m
cards.why: Forgetting to halve the distance is the usual error in pulse-echo questions.
steps: Distance travelled by the pulse: vt=1500×4.0×10−5=0.060 m\displaystyle vt = 1500 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-5} = 0.060\ \text{m}vt=1500×4.0×10−5=0.060 m.
That is there and back, so halve it.
Depth =0.030 m\displaystyle = 0.030\ \text{m}=0.030 m

cards.q: State two things that limit the amount of detail a pulse-echo technique can give.
cards.a: The wavelength: objects much smaller than the wavelength are not resolved, so a shorter wavelength shows finer detail. The duration of the pulses: a pulse must be short enough that its echo returns before the next pulse is sent and does not overlap it.
